**The Weight of a Thousand Words**

The first time I realized words could carry weight, I was twelve. My father had just left, and my mother sat me down at the kitchen table, her hands trembling around a cup of tea that had long gone cold. She said, *"Words are like stones, darling. You can build a bridge with them, or you can drop them into a well and never hear the splash."*

I didn’t understand then. Words were just sounds, shapes on paper. But now, years later, I know what she meant. Words are the invisible architecture of our lives—they shape us, break us, and sometimes, if we’re lucky, they lift us up.

I’ve written a thousand words today. Some were light, dancing across the page like fireflies. Others were heavy, dragging behind them the weight of memories I’d rather forget. But every one of them mattered.

I wrote about the time I lost my best friend to silence. Not death—just silence. The kind that settles between two people like dust on an old bookshelf. We stopped speaking because we ran out of words, or maybe because we were afraid of the ones we had left. I wrote about the guilt of not trying harder, the way regret tastes like metal on the tongue.

I wrote about love, too. Not the grand, sweeping kind from movies, but the quiet, stubborn kind that lingers in the way someone folds your laundry or leaves the coffee just the way you like it. I wrote about the first time I saw the ocean and how it made me feel small and infinite all at once. I wrote about the way my grandmother’s hands smelled like flour and vanilla, and how I still miss her even though she’s been gone for years.

I wrote about failure. The exams I didn’t pass, the jobs I didn’t get, the dreams that slipped through my fingers like sand. I wrote about the nights I spent staring at the ceiling, wondering if I was enough. I wrote about the mornings I woke up and decided, *Today, I will try again.*

I wrote about the future, too. Not as a fixed destination, but as something fluid, something I could shape with my choices. I wrote about the person I want to be—kinder, braver, more patient. I wrote about the things I want to do: travel, write a book, learn to play the piano, plant a garden.

And then, when I had nothing left to say, I wrote about silence. The kind that isn’t empty, but full—full of all the words we haven’t said yet, all the stories we’re still waiting to tell.

A thousand words. A thousand thoughts, a thousand feelings, a thousand fragments of a life still unfolding. And in the end, I realized something: words don’t just carry weight. They *are* weight. They are the measure of who we are, the proof of what we’ve lived.

So I’ll keep writing. Not because I have to, but because I can. Because every word is a step forward, a bridge built, a stone cast into the well of the unknown.

And maybe, just maybe, someone will hear the splash.
